target: Auf Wiedersehen, es war schön.
english: Goodbye, it was nice.
old: 'Auf Wiedersehen' is the formal goodbye.
focus: Add the informal contrast (Tschüss) so the formality stake is concrete; stay anchored on 'Auf Wiedersehen'.

target: Wir essen zusammen zu Mittag.
english: We eat lunch together.
old: 'Zu Mittag essen' = to have lunch.
focus: 'zu Mittag essen' is literally 'to eat at midday' – German needs no word for 'lunch' here; make the literal logic the hook.

target: Wir haben kein Geld mehr.
english: We have no more money.
old: 'kein' negates nouns directly – replaces the indefinite article with matching endings.
focus: English 'no / not any' = kein, never 'nicht ein' – anchor 'kein Geld mehr' and make the telling distinct from the two sibling kein tips.

target: Hey, was machst du hier?
english: Hey, what are you doing here?
old: Default to `Sie` with anyone you would address as Mr/Mrs in English. Wait for them to suggest `wir können uns duzen` (let us switch to du).
focus: Strip the backticks; anchor the casual 'du' in 'was machst du hier' against the default Sie with strangers.

target: Die Kinder haben morgen schulfrei.
english: The children don't have school tomorrow.
old: 'Schulfrei haben' – 'to have a school holiday' – a common compound adjective.
focus: 'schulfrei' is literally 'school-free' – the productive -frei pattern (alkoholfrei, autofrei); drop the 'compound adjective' jargon.

target: Sie hat Heimweh nach ihrer Familie.
english: She misses her family.
old: 'Heimweh haben' – 'to be homesick' – germans 'have homesickness'.
focus: You HAVE homesickness in German – 'Heimweh haben', literally 'home-ache'; fix the lowercase 'germans' and tighten the choppy triple-dash phrasing.

target: Können wir bitte die Speisekarte haben?
english: Can we please have the menu?
old: Modal verb in position 2, main verb at the end. Ich muss morgen früh aufstehen (I have to get up early tomorrow). Brackets the sentence.
focus: Modal bracket using THIS card: 'Können' opens, 'haben' waits at the end – drop the foreign aufstehen example and the 'position 2' claim, which is wrong for this question.

target: Sie ist nach der Arbeit sofort eingeschlafen.
english: She fell asleep immediately after work.
old: Separable with 'sein': ein·schlafen → ist ein·ge·schlafen.
focus: ge- squeezes INSIDE separable verbs: 'eingeschlafen' = ein + ge + schlafen; replace the middle-dot notation with plain text and pick this one rule.

target: Ich habe Hunger, lass uns etwas essen gehen.
english: I am hungry, let's go eat something.
old: 'Hunger haben' – germans 'have hunger' rather than 'being hungry'.
focus: 'Hunger haben' – you have hunger in German, you aren't hungry; fix the lowercase 'germans' and sharpen the hook.

target: Ich lerne seit einem Jahr Deutsch.
english: I have been learning German for a year.
old: After mit / aus / bei / nach / von / zu / seit / gegenüber, the article shifts to dem (m/n), der (f), den (plural). Always – no exceptions.
focus: 'seit einem Jahr' + present 'lerne' = English 'have been learning' – German uses present tense with seit; replace the stamped dative-preposition list with this card's real trap.

target: Sie erzählt gern Geschichten aus ihrer Kindheit.
english: She likes to tell stories from her childhood.
old: 'Gern(e)' after a verb means 'like to' – 'Ich lese gern' = 'I like to read'. It is an adverb, not a verb.
focus: gern after a verb = 'like to' – keep that insight but anchor the worked example in this card's 'erzählt gern Geschichten', not the generic 'Ich lese gern'

target: Wir haben leider keinen Platz mehr im Restaurant.
english: Unfortunately we have no more room in the restaurant.
old: 'keinen' negates nouns directly – replaces the indefinite article with matching endings.
focus: kein (not nicht) negates nouns – anchor in this card's 'keinen Platz mehr' and note English 'no more room' maps to kein, differentiating from the 2 sibling tellings

target: Er wartet schon seit einer Stunde auf den Bus.
english: He has been waiting for the bus for an hour.
old: 'Schon' (already) is a modal particle that adds emphasis – 'Wie lange wohnst du schon hier?' implies ongoing duration.
focus: seit/schon + PRESENT tense = English 'has been ...ing' – anchor in 'wartet schon seit einer Stunde'; drop the 'modal particle' jargon and the generic example

target: Um drei Uhr nachmittags gibt es Kaffee und Kuchen.
english: At three in the afternoon there is coffee and cake.
old: German is V2: the conjugated verb is always the second element. `Heute gehe ich ins Kino` (today go I to-the cinema) – nOT `Heute ich gehe`. Whatever comes first, the verb is right after.
focus: V2: verb stays second after a fronted time phrase – anchor with this card's 'Um drei Uhr nachmittags gibt es'; strip backticks and the 'nOT' typo, cut the generic Kino example

target: Meine Tante liest jeden Abend ihren Enkelkindern eine lange Geschichte vor.
english: My aunt reads her grandchildren a long story every evening.
old: 'lesen' stem-vowel change: e→ie: 'liest'; separable: 'vorlesen'.
focus: one rule only: separable 'vorlesen' splits, prefix lands at the sentence end – anchor in 'liest ... vor'; cut the stem-change half

target: Ich empfehle Ihnen, ein Tagesticket für den gesamten Nahverkehr zu kaufen.
english: I recommend buying a day ticket for all local transport.
old: für always takes the direct-object form: für mich (for me), für dich (for you), für den Mann (for the man). No extra preposition needed.
focus: für always takes accusative and this card shows it visibly – anchor in 'für den gesamten Nahverkehr' (den, not der); cut the generic example list and the confusing 'no extra preposition' line

target: Heute Nachmittag holt mein Vater uns vom Bahnhof ab.
english: This afternoon my father is picking us up from the train station.
old: Starting with 'heute' (today) triggers inversion: 'Heute gehe ich...' – the verb must remain in second position.
focus: fronted 'Heute Nachmittag' forces verb-subject inversion – use this card's 'Heute Nachmittag holt mein Vater' as the worked example instead of the generic 'Heute gehe ich'

target: Er nimmt das Taxi, weil der letzte Bus schon abgefahren ist.
english: He takes a taxi because the last bus has already left.
old: Subordinating conjunctions (`dass`, `weil`, `wenn`, `ob`, `obwohl`) send the verb to the end of the clause: `Ich weiß, dass er morgen kommt`.
focus: weil sends the verb to the clause end – anchor in this card's 'weil der letzte Bus schon abgefahren ist'; strip backticks and the generic dass example

target: Warme Suppe mit frischem Brot ist an kalten Wintertagen das perfekte Essen.
english: Warm soup with fresh bread is the perfect meal on cold winter days.
old: No article: adj. takes strong endings showing gender and case.
focus: with no article, the adjective carries the case ending itself – anchor in 'mit frischem Brot' (the -em the missing article would have shown); expand the telegraphic phrasing, avoid 'strong endings' jargon

target: Hast du Geschwister?
english: Do you have siblings?
old: Yes/no question – verb takes V1 position. German doesn't need a 'do' auxiliary.
focus: German yes/no questions need no 'do' – 'Hast du Geschwister?' is literally 'Have you siblings?'; quote the card and lose the 'V1 position' jargon

target: Wir sind begeistert von der neuen Ausstellung.
english: We are excited about the new exhibition.
old: 'Begeistert von' uses dative – 'excited/enthusiastic about'.
focus: The real trap is the preposition: excited ABOUT = begeistert VON (not ueber) – anchor 'begeistert von der neuen Ausstellung'; drop the dative aside (von is always dative).

target: Du träumst von einer Weltreise.
english: You dream of a trip around the world.
old: Chant it: mit, aus, bei, nach, von, zu, seit, gegenüber. After any of these the article goes to dem / der / den. No thinking required.
focus: Cut the chant-list; anchor to this card: 'von einer Weltreise' – von always takes dative, so eine becomes einer.

target: Wir wohnen seit fünf Jahren hier.
english: We have been living here for five years.
old: 'seit' (since/for) always governs the dative case – no exceptions.
focus: The bigger trap on this card: 'Wir wohnen seit fuenf Jahren' uses PRESENT tense where English says 'have been living' – German present + seit covers ongoing duration.

target: Du musst lernen, auch mal fünf gerade sein zu lassen.
english: You have to learn to let some things slide.
old: 'fünf gerade sein lassen' = to turn a blind eye / be lenient.
focus: Give the literal image instead of re-glossing: 'fuenf gerade sein lassen' = let five be an even number – accept small wrongness rather than correcting everything.

target: Wir haben auf der ganzen Reise kein einziges günstiges Hotelzimmer gefunden.
english: We didn't find a single affordable hotel room on the entire trip.
old: 'kein' negates indef. article: 'ein Zimmer' → 'kein Zimmer'.
focus: English 'not a' = kein, never nicht ein – anchor to 'kein einziges guenstiges Hotelzimmer'; spell out indef., no arrow notation.

target: Hast du Angst vor Spinnen?
english: Are you afraid of spiders?
old: 'Angst haben vor' uses 'haben' + dative – germans 'have fear' rather than 'being afraid'.
focus: Germans HAVE fear: 'Angst haben vor' – keep that hook, fix lowercase 'germans' and the garbled 'rather than being afraid' phrasing, anchor 'Angst vor Spinnen'.

target: Ich bin fest davon überzeugt.
english: I am firmly convinced of that.
old: 'Überzeugt sein von' – 'to be convinced of' – always with dative.
focus: The interesting token is 'davon' – da- fuses with the preposition ueberzeugt pairs with (von) to mean 'of it/that'; lead with that, drop the bare dative claim.

target: Bist du sicher, dass das stimmt?
english: Are you sure that is correct?
old: 'Dass' (that) introduces a noun clause – verb goes to the end. Often replaceable by dropping 'dass' and using V2 order.
focus: One rule only: dass sends the verb to the clause end – anchor 'dass das stimmt'; cut the second rule about dropping dass for V2.

target: Ich bin allergisch gegen Nüsse und Erdbeeren.
english: I am allergic to nuts and strawberries.
old: 'gegen' (against) always takes accusative – no exceptions.
focus: The real trap is 'allergisch gegen' – German says allergic AGAINST, not 'to'; gegen+accusative is at most a side note

target: Trotz des schlechten Wetters gehen wir wandern.
english: Despite the bad weather we are going hiking.
old: V2 rule: 'Trotz des schlechten Wetters' is one element in position 1.
focus: The whole phrase 'Trotz des schlechten Wetters' fills slot 1, so the verb comes straight after: gehen wir, not wir gehen – spell out the consequence, skip the bare 'V2 rule' label

target: Ich trinke gern kalten Kaffee im Sommer.
english: I like to drink cold coffee in summer.
old: No article (masc. acc): '-en' ending – adjective shows the case itself.
focus: With no article the adjective carries the case ending itself: 'kalten Kaffee' shows the masculine accusative -en – quote the card, plain words instead of '(masc. acc)' notation

target: Der Wecker klingelt jeden Morgen um sechs Uhr.
english: The alarm clock rings every morning at six.
old: Accusative changes 'der' to 'den' and 'ein' to 'einen' (masc. only).
focus: 'jeden Morgen' is accusative because bare time expressions take accusative – that's why jeder becomes jeden; the current der→den/ein→einen tip never touches the card

target: Frisches Brot aus der Bäckerei schmeckt am besten.
english: Fresh bread from the bakery tastes the best.
old: No article (neut. nom): '-es' ending – adjective must show gender/case.
focus: No article means the adjective shows gender/case itself: 'Frisches Brot' takes the -es that 'das' would otherwise carry – plain words, no '(neut. nom)' notation

target: Ich bin fix und fertig nach dem langen Arbeitstag.
english: I am completely exhausted after the long workday.
old: 'Fix und fertig sein' – to be completely exhausted/done in.
focus: 'fertig' alone means both 'finished' and 'wiped out' – 'fix und fertig' intensifies it; give that logic instead of re-stating the English translation

target: Der Kuchen, den meine Mutter backt, ist unglaublich lecker.
english: The cake my mother bakes is incredibly delicious.
old: 'den' (acc. masc./dat. pl.) introduces a relative clause – its case depends on its role within that clause.
focus: 'den' is accusative because of its role INSIDE its own clause (meine Mutter backt den Kuchen) – keep that insight, cut the '(acc. masc./dat. pl.)' notation clutter

target: Sie hat das Heft in der Hand und bestimmt, wohin die Reise geht.
english: She has the reins in hand and decides where the journey goes.
old: 'Das Heft in der Hand haben' – to be in charge/in control.
focus: 'Heft' here means hilt/handle, not notebook – a two-meanings landmine; lead with that, not a re-gloss the English field already gives

target: Sie hat zwei linke Hände, wenn es ums Heimwerken geht.
english: She is all thumbs when it comes to DIY.
old: 'Zwei linke Hände haben' – to be clumsy with manual work.
focus: Give the literal image: 'zwei linke Hände' = two left hands, German's version of 'all thumbs' – the current tip only repeats the meaning

target: Er half seiner älteren Nachbarin beim Tragen der schweren Einkaufstüten.
english: He helped his elderly neighbor carry the heavy shopping bags.
old: 'seiner Nachbarin' = dative fem.; 'helfen' takes dative object.
focus: 'helfen' takes a dative object – in German you help TO someone: er half seiner Nachbarin; cut the '= dative fem.' notation, add the English-contrast hook

target: Heißer Tee mit frischem Ingwer hilft bei einer starken Erkältung.
english: Hot tea with fresh ginger helps with a bad cold.
old: Without article: 'Heißer' takes strong nom. masc. ending '-er'.
focus: Without an article the adjective takes the ending itself: 'Heißer Tee' – say it in plain words, no 'strong nom. masc.' jargon

target: Bitte hör mir jetzt genau zu, das ist wirklich sehr wichtig.
english: Please listen to me carefully now, this is really very important.
old: Separable: 'zuhören' – 'hör...zu'.
focus: Separable verbs split in commands – 'zuhören' becomes 'hör ... zu' with the prefix stranded at the end; give the intuition, not just the 'Separable:' label

target: Sie hat ein Brett vor dem Kopf und sieht die offensichtliche Lösung nicht.
english: She has a mental block and doesn't see the obvious solution.
old: 'ein Brett vor dem Kopf haben' = to have a mental block.
focus: Give the literal image: 'ein Brett vor dem Kopf' = a board in front of your head, so you can't see what's right there – don't just repeat 'mental block'

target: Du wirst das schon schaffen.
english: You will manage that.
old: 'Schon' adds reassurance.
focus: 'schon' here is a reassuring particle ('you'll manage alright'), NOT 'already' – name the two-meanings landmine; the current 4-word tip has no anchor or example

target: Ich bin noch nicht fertig.
english: I'm not finished yet.
old: 'Nicht' placement follows strict rules – typically before what it negates, and always before the final verb element (participle/infinitive/prefix).
focus: 'noch nicht' = not yet, literally 'still not' – anchor on that phrase from the card; drop the generic nicht-placement rulebook that doesn't fit this sentence

target: Wir werden den Garten gestalten.
english: We will design the garden.
old: "The" forms by role: subject = der/die/das, direct object = den/die/das, after a few prepositions = dem/der/dem. Worth memorising as a small table.
focus: den Garten shows der becoming den for the direct object – teach that one visible switch, drop the memorise-a-table dump.

target: Er hat keine Ahnung davon.
english: He has no idea about it.
old: kein = no / not a. Used to negate a noun. Ich habe kein Geld (I have no money), not ich habe nicht Geld. Use kein instead of nicht with nouns.
focus: kein-vs-nicht is the real trap – anchor it in this card's 'keine Ahnung' instead of the stock kein Geld example.

target: Du hast keinen Grund zur Sorge.
english: You have no reason to worry.
old: `kein` agrees like the indefinite article `ein`: keinen (m acc), keine (f), keinem (m dat), etc. Same endings as ein/eine just with k- in front.
focus: keinen Grund shows kein wearing ein's endings (masc accusative -en) – quote it, kill the backticks and the case list.
